claim: Cold- and heat stress sensitivity of fugu5 mutants lacking the major H+-PPase isoform AVP1 is correlated with reduced SUMOylation.
source: We show here, that both cold- and heat stress sensitivity of fugu5 mutants lacking the major H+-PPase isoform AVP1 is correlated with reduced SUMOylation.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing reduced SUMOylation in fugu5 mutants under stress conditions (Figures 3 and 4).

claim: Increased PPi concentrations interfere with SUMOylation in yeast.
source: In addition, we show that increased PPi concentrations interfere with SUMOylation in yeast
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from yeast showing reduced SUMOylation upon PPi accumulation (Figure 5).

claim: SUMO activating E1-enzymes are inhibited by micromolar concentrations of PPi in a non-competitive manner.
source: we provide evidence that SUMO activating E1-enzymes are inhibited by micromolar concentrations of PPi in a non-competitive manner.
evidence: The manuscript presents in vitro assay data showing E1 enzyme inhibition by PPi (Figure 6), though the mode is described as 'mixed' rather than 'non-competitive' in the results.

claim: PPi is a byproduct of macromolecule biosynthesis.
source: Pyrophosphate (PPi), a byproduct of macromolecule biosynthesis is maintained at low levels by soluble inorganic pyrophosphatases (sPPase) found in all eukaryotes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about PPi production during biosynthetic reactions.

claim: Soluble inorganic pyrophosphatases (sPPase) are found in all eukaryotes.
source: Pyrophosphate (PPi), a byproduct of macromolecule biosynthesis is maintained at low levels by soluble inorganic pyrophosphatases (sPPase) found in all eukaryotes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the ubiquity of sPPases.

claim: H+-pumping pyrophosphatases (H+-PPase) in plants convert the energy present in PPi into an electrochemical gradient.
source: In plants, H+-pumping pyrophosphatases (H+-PPase) convert the substantial energy present in PPi into an electrochemical gradient.
evidence: This is established knowledge about plant H+-PPases, also supported by citations in the introduction (Maeshima, 2000).

claim: About 200 metabolic reactions use ATP as an adenylating reagent rather than a phosphorylating reagent, leading to the release of inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi).
source: In about 200 metabolic reactions ATP is not used as a phosphorylating but as an adenylating reagent leading to the release of inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ferjani et al., 2014 and Heinonen, 2001.

claim: The biosynthesis of DNA, RNA, proteins and polysaccharides releases large amounts of PPi.
source: Most prominently, the biosynthesis of many macromolecules including DNA, RNA, proteins and polysaccharides releases large amounts of PPi (Ferjani et al., 2014; Heinonen, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ferjani et al., 2014 and Heinonen, 2001.

claim: Efficient biosynthesis of macromolecules requires that PPi is immediately destroyed to prevent back-reactions.
source: Given the substantial free energy of PPi, the efficient biosynthesis of macromolecules requires that PPi is immediately destroyed to prevent the respective back-reactions (Kornberg, 1962).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kornberg, 1962.

claim: Loss of sPPase function causes lethality in yeast.
source: Loss of sPPase function causes lethality in yeast (Lundin et al., 1991)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lundin et al., 1991.

claim: Loss of sPPase function causes lethality in C. elegans.
source: Loss of sPPase function causes lethality in yeast (Lundin et al., 1991) and C. elegans (Ko et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ko et al., 2007.

claim: Lethality from loss of sPPase is presumably due to accumulation of PPi inhibiting the biosynthesis of macromolecules.
source: Loss of sPPase function causes lethality in yeast (Lundin et al., 1991) and C. elegans (Ko et al., 2007) presumably due to accumulation of PPi inhibiting the biosynthesis of macromolecules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known role of PPi in biosynthetic reactions.

claim: Arabidopsis encodes six sPPase-paralogs (PPa1-PPa6).
source: Arabidopsis encodes six sPPase-paralogs (PPa1-PPa6) of which only PPa6 is localized in plastids whereas all others are cytosolic (Gutiérrez-Luna et al., 2016; Segami et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gutiérrez-Luna et al., 2016 and Segami et al., 2018.

claim: Only PPa6 is localized in plastids whereas all other Arabidopsis sPPases are cytosolic.
source: Arabidopsis encodes six sPPase-paralogs (PPa1-PPa6) of which only PPa6 is localized in plastids whereas all others are cytosolic (Gutiérrez-Luna et al., 2016; Segami et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gutiérrez-Luna et al., 2016 and Segami et al., 2018.

claim: The PPase activity of Arabidopsis sPPases is rather low.
source: However, their PPase activity is rather low and even the loss of the four ubiquitously expressed isoforms does not cause visible phenotypic alterations (Segami et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Segami et al., 2018.

claim: Loss of the four ubiquitously expressed Arabidopsis sPPase isoforms does not cause visible phenotypic alterations.
source: However, their PPase activity is rather low and even the loss of the four ubiquitously expressed isoforms does not cause visible phenotypic alterations (Segami et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Segami et al., 2018.

claim: Expression of E. coli sPPase severely affects plant growth via alterations in carbon partitioning between source and sink organs.
source: In contrast, expression of E. coli sPPase severely affects plant growth via alterations in carbon partitioning between source and sink organs caused by the inhibition of several plant enzymes involved in carbohydrate metabolism that use PPi as an energy source (Geigenberger et al., 1998; Sonnewald, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Geigenberger et al., 1998 and Sonnewald, 1992.

claim: Expression of E. coli sPPase inhibits several plant enzymes involved in carbohydrate metabolism that use PPi as an energy source.
source: In contrast, expression of E. coli sPPase severely affects plant growth via alterations in carbon partitioning between source and sink organs caused by the inhibition of several plant enzymes involved in carbohydrate metabolism that use PPi as an energy source (Geigenberger et al., 1998; Sonnewald, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Geigenberger et al., 1998 and Sonnewald, 1992.

claim: Plants contain membrane-bound proton-pumping pyrophosphatases (H+-PPase) at the tonoplast and in the Golgi.
source: Importantly, in addition to soluble PPases, plants contain membrane-bound proton-pumping pyrophosphatases (H+-PPase) at the tonoplast and in the Golgi that convert the energy otherwise released as heat into a proton-gradient (Maeshima, 2000; Segami et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Maeshima, 2000 and Segami et al., 2010.

claim: Plant H+-PPases convert the energy otherwise released as heat into a proton-gradient.
source: Importantly, in addition to soluble PPases, plants contain membrane-bound proton-pumping pyrophosphatases (H+-PPase) at the tonoplast and in the Golgi that convert the energy otherwise released as heat into a proton-gradient (Maeshima, 2000; Segami et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Maeshima, 2000 and Segami et al., 2010.

claim: Mutants lacking the tonoplast H+-PPase AVP1 were identified based on their compensatory cell enlargement phenotype and were named fugu5.
source: Mutants lacking the tonoplast H+-PPase AVP1 (Arabidopsis vacuolar H+-PPase) were identified based on their compensatory cell enlargement phenotype and were thus named fugu5 (after the japanese term for the pufferfish; Ferjani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ferjani et al., 2011.

claim: The fugu5 phenotype could be rescued by growth in the presence of exogenous sucrose.
source: The fact that the fugu5 phenotype could be rescued either by growth in the presence of exogenous sucrose or the expression of the yeast sPPase IPP1 showed clearly that altered PPi levels and not reduced H+-pumping are causative (Asaoka et al., 2016; Ferjani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Asaoka et al., 2016 and Ferjani et al., 2011.

claim: The fugu5 phenotype could be rescued by expression of the yeast sPPase IPP1.
source: The fact that the fugu5 phenotype could be rescued either by growth in the presence of exogenous sucrose or the expression of the yeast sPPase IPP1 showed clearly that altered PPi levels and not reduced H+-pumping are causative (Asaoka et al., 2016; Ferjani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Asaoka et al., 2016 and Ferjani et al., 2011.

claim: Altered PPi levels and not reduced H+-pumping are causative for the fugu5 phenotype.
source: The fact that the fugu5 phenotype could be rescued either by growth in the presence of exogenous sucrose or the expression of the yeast sPPase IPP1 showed clearly that altered PPi levels and not reduced H+-pumping are causative (Asaoka et al., 2016; Ferjani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Asaoka et al., 2016 and Ferjani et al., 2011, and by inference from the rescue experiments.

claim: Vacuolar pH is only mildly affected in fugu5 mutants.
source: Indeed, vacuolar pH is only mildly affected in fugu5 mutants indicating that the H+-pumping ATPase (V-ATPase) present at the tonoplast is largely sufficient for vacuolar acidification (Ferjani et al., 2011; Kriegel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ferjani et al., 2011 and Kriegel et al., 2015.

claim: The H+-pumping ATPase (V-ATPase) present at the tonoplast is largely sufficient for vacuolar acidification.
source: Indeed, vacuolar pH is only mildly affected in fugu5 mutants indicating that the H+-pumping ATPase (V-ATPase) present at the tonoplast is largely sufficient for vacuolar acidification (Ferjani et al., 2011; Kriegel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the mild pH effect in fugu5 mutants and supported by citations to Ferjani et al., 2011 and Kriegel et al., 2015.

claim: Loss of both vacuolar proton-pumps leads to a much more severe phenotype and defect in vacuolar acidification than loss of the tonoplast V-ATPase alone.
source: However, loss of both vacuolar proton-pumps leads to a much more severe phenotype and defect in vacuolar acidification than loss of the tonoplast V-ATPase alone (Kriegel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kriegel et al., 2015.

claim: AVP1 serves as a backup system for the V-ATPase under ATP-limiting conditions like anoxia or cold stress.
source: It has indeed been discussed that AVP1 serves as a backup system for the V-ATPase in particular under ATP-limiting conditions like anoxia or cold stress (Maeshima, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maeshima, 2000.

claim: During cold acclimation plants accumulate cryoprotectants including sugars in their vacuoles.
source: During cold acclimation plants accumulate cryoprotectants including sugars in their vacuoles and activity of both proton-pumps is upregulated leading to improved freezing tolerance (Schulze et al., 2012; Thomashow, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schulze et al., 2012 and Thomashow, 1999.

claim: Activity of both proton-pumps is upregulated during cold acclimation leading to improved freezing tolerance.
source: During cold acclimation plants accumulate cryoprotectants including sugars in their vacuoles and activity of both proton-pumps is upregulated leading to improved freezing tolerance (Schulze et al., 2012; Thomashow, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schulze et al., 2012 and Thomashow, 1999.

claim: Overexpression of AVP1 causes increased plant growth under various abiotic stress conditions including salinity, drought and phosphate starvation.
source: Overexpression of AVP1 has been shown to cause increased plant growth under various abiotic stress conditions including salinity, drought and phosphate starvation but the underlying mechanism remained unclear (Gaxiola et al., 2012; Park et al., 2005; Schilling et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gaxiola et al., 2012, Park et al., 2005, and Schilling et al., 2017.

claim: Attachment of SUMO to substrate proteins plays a central role in the response to a broad set of stress responses including those affected by AVP1 overexpression.
source: Attachment of the small ubiquitin-related modifier SUMO to substrate proteins plays a central role in the response to a broad set of stress responses including the ones affected by AVP1 overexpression (Castro et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Castro et al., 2012.

claim: Modification of target proteins by SUMO-conjugation proceeds via a three-step mechanism involving E1, E2, and E3 enzymes.
source: Modification of target proteins by SUMO-conjugation proceeds via a three-step mechanism. First the SUMO moiety is adenylated and then bound via a high-energy thioester linkage to the heterodimeric SUMO-activating enzyme (E1) leading to the release of PPi. Next, the activated SUMO is transferred to the SUMO-conjugating enzyme E2 and finally, assisted by SUMO-protein ligase (E3), donated to a large set of substrate proteins (Flotho and Melchior, 2013; Johnson, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Flotho and Melchior, 2013 and Johnson, 2004.

claim: The SUMO E1 activation step releases PPi.
source: First the SUMO moiety is adenylated and then bound via a high-energy thioester linkage to the heterodimeric SUMO-activating enzyme (E1) leading to the release of PPi.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the SUMO conjugation mechanism.

claim: ICE1 is positively regulated by SUMOylation.
source: In Arabidopsis, the key transcriptional regulator of the cold response Inducer of CBF expression 1 (ICE1) as well as the Heat shock factor A2 (HSFA2) have been shown to be positively regulated by SUMOylation (Cohen-Peer et al., 2010; Miura et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cohen-Peer et al., 2010 and Miura et al., 2007.

claim: Heat shock factor A2 (HSFA2) is positively regulated by SUMOylation.
source: In Arabidopsis, the key transcriptional regulator of the cold response Inducer of CBF expression 1 (ICE1) as well as the Heat shock factor A2 (HSFA2) have been shown to be positively regulated by SUMOylation (Cohen-Peer et al., 2010; Miura et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cohen-Peer et al., 2010 and Miura et al., 2007.

claim: AVP1 contributes to cold acclimation.
source: In this study, we report that AVP1 contributes to both cold acclimation and heat tolerance
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 1 and 2).

claim: AVP1 contributes to heat tolerance.
source: In this study, we report that AVP1 contributes to both cold acclimation and heat tolerance
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 4).

claim: The rapid increase in SUMOylation common to both cold and heat stress responses is missing in the absence of AVP1.
source: we show that the rapid increase in SUMOylation common to both stress responses is missing in the absence of AVP1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 3 and 4).

claim: Accumulation of PPi in plants inhibits the SUMO E1 activating enzyme.
source: Furthermore, we provide evidence that accumulation of PPi in plants, yeast and mammals inhibits the SUMO E1 activating enzyme in turn affecting the fate, localization or function of a large number of proteins during cellular stress responses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 3-6).

claim: Accumulation of PPi in yeast inhibits the SUMO E1 activating enzyme.
source: Furthermore, we provide evidence that accumulation of PPi in plants, yeast and mammals inhibits the SUMO E1 activating enzyme in turn affecting the fate, localization or function of a large number of proteins during cellular stress responses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 5 and 6).

claim: Accumulation of PPi in mammals inhibits the SUMO E1 activating enzyme.
source: Furthermore, we provide evidence that accumulation of PPi in plants, yeast and mammals inhibits the SUMO E1 activating enzyme in turn affecting the fate, localization or function of a large number of proteins during cellular stress responses.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro data using human E1 enzyme (Figure 6).

claim: Upregulation of ATP-hydrolysis by the V-ATPase during cold acclimation depends on the presence and activity of the V-PPase.
source: We have shown previously that upregulation of ATP-hydrolysis by the V-ATPase during cold acclimation depends on the presence and the activity of the V-PPase (Kriegel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kriegel et al., 2015.

claim: Both ATP- and PPi-dependent proton-pumping are increased in wild-type during cold-acclimation.
source: Both ATP- and PPi-dependent proton-pumping are increased in wild-type (wt) and UBQ:AVP1 during cold-acclimation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Both ATP- and PPi-dependent proton-pumping are increased in UBQ:AVP1 during cold-acclimation.
source: Both ATP- and PPi-dependent proton-pumping are increased in wild-type (wt) and UBQ:AVP1 during cold-acclimation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: PPi-dependent proton-pumping was undetectable in fugu5-1.
source: As expected PPi-dependent proton-pumping was undetectable in fugu5-1
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ATP-dependent proton-pumping was reduced in fugu5-1 compared to wt.
source: but ATP-dependent proton-pumping was also reduced in fugu5-1 compared to wt and increased only marginally upon cold-acclimation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ATP-dependent proton-pumping increased only marginally in fugu5-1 upon cold-acclimation.
source: but ATP-dependent proton-pumping was also reduced in fugu5-1 compared to wt and increased only marginally upon cold-acclimation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Vacuolar pH drops by 0.1 pH-units in wt during cold acclimation.
source: As a consequence of cold-induced proton-pump stimulation, vacuolar pH drops by 0.1 pH-units in wt and UBQ:AVP1 but not in fugu5-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Vacuolar pH drops by 0.1 pH-units in UBQ:AVP1 during cold acclimation.
source: As a consequence of cold-induced proton-pump stimulation, vacuolar pH drops by 0.1 pH-units in wt and UBQ:AVP1 but not in fugu5-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Vacuolar pH does not drop in fugu5-1 during cold acclimation.
source: As a consequence of cold-induced proton-pump stimulation, vacuolar pH drops by 0.1 pH-units in wt and UBQ:AVP1 but not in fugu5-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The seedling phenotype of fugu5-1 is rescued by expression of the yeast soluble PPase IPP1 under control of the AVP1-promoter during the seedling stage.
source: Whereas the seedling phenotype of fugu5-1 is rescued by expression of the yeast soluble PPase IPP1 under control of the AVP1-promoter during the seedling stage (Ferjani et al., 2011), the adult growth phenotype of plants grown in short day was not rescued (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ferjani et al., 2011 and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The adult growth phenotype of fugu5-1 plants grown in short day was not rescued by expression of IPP1 under control of the AVP1-promoter.
source: Whereas the seedling phenotype of fugu5-1 is rescued by expression of the yeast soluble PPase IPP1 under control of the AVP1-promoter during the seedling stage (Ferjani et al., 2011), the adult growth phenotype of plants grown in short day was not rescued (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: PPa5-GFP was located in the cytosol as well as in the nucleus.
source: In the resulting transgenic lines PPa5-GFP was located in the cytosol as well as in the nucleus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The seedling phenotype of fugu5-1 was fully rescued by UBQ:PPa5-GFP.
source: and the seedling (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) as well as the adult phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D+E) of fugu5-1 were fully rescued.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The adult phenotype of fugu5-1 was fully rescued by UBQ:PPa5-GFP.
source: and the seedling (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) as well as the adult phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D+E) of fugu5-1 were fully rescued.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D+E.

claim: PPa5-GFP accumulated to much higher levels in fugu5-1 than in wt.
source: Interestingly, PPa5-GFP accumulated to much higher levels in fugu5-1 than in wt (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G) indicating that the fugu5-1 mutation influences either protein stability or transcript levels of PPa5-GFP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G.

claim: The fugu5-1 mutation influences either protein stability or transcript levels of PPa5-GFP.
source: Interestingly, PPa5-GFP accumulated to much higher levels in fugu5-1 than in wt (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G) indicating that the fugu5-1 mutation influences either protein stability or transcript levels of PPa5-GFP.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of higher PPa5-GFP levels in fugu5-1.

claim: Survival rate after freezing without prior cold acclimation was comparable in all genotypes.
source: Both survival rate and ion release as a measure of freezing tolerance was comparable in all genotypes exposed to freezing without prior cold acclimation (Figure 1A + B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A + B.

claim: Ion release as a measure of freezing tolerance was comparable in all genotypes exposed to freezing without prior cold acclimation.
source: Both survival rate and ion release as a measure of freezing tolerance was comparable in all genotypes exposed to freezing without prior cold acclimation (Figure 1A + B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A + B.

claim: Cold acclimation significantly improved freezing tolerance in wt to a much higher extent than in fugu5-1 plants.
source: Cold acclimation via exposure to 4°C for 4 days significantly improved freezing tolerance in wt to a much higher extent than in fugu5-1 plants and expression of PPa5 fully rescued the hypersensitivity to cold (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Expression of PPa5 fully rescued the hypersensitivity to cold in fugu5-1.
source: Cold acclimation via exposure to 4°C for 4 days significantly improved freezing tolerance in wt to a much higher extent than in fugu5-1 plants and expression of PPa5 fully rescued the hypersensitivity to cold (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mutants lacking one or several sPPases are less freezing tolerant prior to cold exposure.
source: Conversely, mutants lacking one or several sPPases (Segami et al., 2018) are less freezing tolerant prior to cold exposure but respond like wt after cold-acclimation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and citation to Segami et al., 2018.

claim: Mutants lacking one or several sPPases respond like wt after cold-acclimation.
source: Conversely, mutants lacking one or several sPPases (Segami et al., 2018) are less freezing tolerant prior to cold exposure but respond like wt after cold-acclimation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cold-induced sugar accumulation is strongly reduced in the fugu5-1 mutant.
source: We thus next compared the accumulation of glucose, fructose and sucrose and found that cold-induced sugar accumulation is indeed strongly reduced in the fugu5-1 mutant but restored by UBQ:PPa5-GFP (Figure 1D–1F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D–1F.

claim: Cold-induced sugar accumulation is restored by UBQ:PPa5-GFP in fugu5-1.
source: We thus next compared the accumulation of glucose, fructose and sucrose and found that cold-induced sugar accumulation is indeed strongly reduced in the fugu5-1 mutant but restored by UBQ:PPa5-GFP (Figure 1D–1F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D–1F.

claim: Accumulation of PPi and not a lack of H+-pumping is responsible for the impaired cold acclimation in fugu5-1.
source: suggesting that accumulation of PPi and not a lack of H+-pumping is responsible for the impaired cold acclimation in fugu5-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of cold acclimation by PPa5-GFP expression.

claim: PPi levels are reduced in the wt during cold-acclimation.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, we found that PPi levels are reduced in the wt during cold-acclimation whereas they increase in fugu5-1 resulting in 2-fold higher levels compared to wt after cold acclimation (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: PPi levels increase in fugu5-1 during cold-acclimation.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, we found that PPi levels are reduced in the wt during cold-acclimation whereas they increase in fugu5-1 resulting in 2-fold higher levels compared to wt after cold acclimation (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: PPi levels in fugu5-1 are 2-fold higher compared to wt after cold acclimation.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, we found that PPi levels are reduced in the wt during cold-acclimation whereas they increase in fugu5-1 resulting in 2-fold higher levels compared to wt after cold acclimation (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Low temperature triggers the expression of the CBF family of transcription factors.
source: Low temperature triggers the expression of the CBF (C-repeat binding factor) family of transcription factors, which in turn activate downstream genes that confer chilling and freezing tolerance (Chinnusamy et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chinnusamy et al., 2007.

claim: CBF transcription factors activate downstream genes that confer chilling and freezing tolerance.
source: Low temperature triggers the expression of the CBF (C-repeat binding factor) family of transcription factors, which in turn activate downstream genes that confer chilling and freezing tolerance (Chinnusamy et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chinnusamy et al., 2007.

claim: PPa1 and PPa4 are rapidly induced after cold exposure.
source: We used qRT-PCR to profile the expression of members of the PPa-gene family over 24 hr after exposure to low temperature (4°C) and found that PPa1 and PPa4 are rapidly induced after cold exposure whereas transcripts of PPa2 and PPa5 accumulated at later time points (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Transcripts of PPa2 and PPa5 accumulated at later time points after cold exposure.
source: We used qRT-PCR to profile the expression of members of the PPa-gene family over 24 hr after exposure to low temperature (4°C) and found that PPa1 and PPa4 are rapidly induced after cold exposure whereas transcripts of PPa2 and PPa5 accumulated at later time points (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Upregulation of sPPase genes suggests that PPi-levels are actively controlled during the early cold acclimation response.
source: Upregulation of sPPase genes suggests that PPi-levels are actively controlled during the early cold acclimation response.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed upregulation of sPPase genes during cold exposure.

claim: Cold-induced upregulation of PPa1, PPa4 and PPa5 is reduced in fugu5.
source: In fugu5, cold-induced upregulation of PPa1, PPa4 and PPa5 is reduced (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Expression of CBF2 was nearly unaffected in fugu5-1.
source: Whereas expression of CBF2 was nearly unaffected, CBF1 and in particular CBF3 induction was found to be strongly reduced in the fugu5-1 mutant (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CBF1 induction was found to be strongly reduced in the fugu5-1 mutant.
source: Whereas expression of CBF2 was nearly unaffected, CBF1 and in particular CBF3 induction was found to be strongly reduced in the fugu5-1 mutant (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CBF3 induction was found to be strongly reduced in the fugu5-1 mutant.
source: Whereas expression of CBF2 was nearly unaffected, CBF1 and in particular CBF3 induction was found to be strongly reduced in the fugu5-1 mutant (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Induction of COR15A, COR78 and GolS3 was found to be strongly reduced throughout the cold response in fugu5-1.
source: Similarly, induction of all three target genes was found to be strongly reduced throughout the cold response (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cold-induction of CBF and target genes was restored when PPa5 was constitutively expressed in the fugu5-1 background.
source: Cold-induction was restored when PPa5 was constitutively expressed in the fugu5-1 background (Figure 2 B + C) indicating that the observed changes in gene expression are caused by reduced PPi-hydrolysis and not by reduced H+-pumping.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 B + C.

claim: The observed changes in gene expression in fugu5-1 are caused by reduced PPi-hydrolysis and not by reduced H+-pumping.
source: Cold-induction was restored when PPa5 was constitutively expressed in the fugu5-1 background (Figure 2 B + C) indicating that the observed changes in gene expression are caused by reduced PPi-hydrolysis and not by reduced H+-pumping.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of gene expression by PPa5 expression.

claim: ICE1 is a direct activator of the cold response.
source: The fast transcriptional response to cold is initiated by ICE1 (Inducer of CBF expression 1), a direct activator that is negatively regulated by ubiquitination-mediated proteolysis and positively regulated by SUMOylation (Dong et al., 2006; Miura et al., 2007; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dong et al., 2006 and Miura et al., 2007.

claim: ICE1 is negatively regulated by ubiquitination-mediated proteolysis.
source: The fast transcriptional response to cold is initiated by ICE1 (Inducer of CBF expression 1), a direct activator that is negatively regulated by ubiquitination-mediated proteolysis and positively regulated by SUMOylation (Dong et al., 2006; Miura et al., 2007; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dong et al., 2006 and Miura et al., 2007.

claim: Two bands corresponding to non-modified (100kD) and modified (130kD) dimer of ICE1 were observed in wild-type.
source: Using a specific antibody to detect ICE1 in total seedling protein extracted in the presence of NEM to inhibit deSUMOylation, we observed two bands in wild-type that are both absent in ice1-2 indicating that they might correspond to a non-modified (100kD) and modified (130kD) dimer of ICE1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The ICE1 monomer (50kD) was only observed when proteins were extracted in the presence of DTT and without NEM.
source: The ICE1 monomer (50kD) was only observed when proteins were extracted in the presence of DTT and without NEM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The modified ICE1 dimer was barely detectable in fugu5-1.
source: In fugu5-1 the modified dimer was barely detectable indicating that either ubiquitination or SUMOylation of ICE1 are affected (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Either ubiquitination or SUMOylation of ICE1 are affected in fugu5-1.
source: In fugu5-1 the modified dimer was barely detectable indicating that either ubiquitination or SUMOylation of ICE1 are affected (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced modified ICE1 dimer in fugu5-1.

claim: ICE1 accumulated after exposure to 4°C for 3 hr in wt.
source: We next compared levels of ICE1 during cold acclimation and found that ICE1 accumulated after exposure to 4°C for 3 hr in wt but was strongly reduced in fugu5-1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ICE1 was strongly reduced in fugu5-1 after exposure to 4°C for 3 hr.
source: We next compared levels of ICE1 during cold acclimation and found that ICE1 accumulated after exposure to 4°C for 3 hr in wt but was strongly reduced in fugu5-1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cold exposure led to a rapid and massive accumulation of SUMO1/2 conjugates in the wild-type.
source: Whereas cold exposure let to a rapid and massive accumulation SUMO1/2 conjugates in the wild-type, this response was absent in fugu5-1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The cold-induced accumulation of SUMO1/2 conjugates was absent in fugu5-1.
source: Whereas cold exposure let to a rapid and massive accumulation SUMO1/2 conjugates in the wild-type, this response was absent in fugu5-1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SUMO levels in fugu5 are reduced to 60% of wt in plants grown at 22°C.
source: Quantification of SUMO levels in two independent fugu5-alleles showed that it is already reduced to 60% of wt in plants grown at 22°C and levels drop to 20% of wt after incubation at 4°C for 3 hr (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: SUMO levels in fugu5 drop to 20% of wt after incubation at 4°C for 3 hr.
source: Quantification of SUMO levels in two independent fugu5-alleles showed that it is already reduced to 60% of wt in plants grown at 22°C and levels drop to 20% of wt after incubation at 4°C for 3 hr (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: SUMOylation is restored to wild-type levels in UBQ:PPa5-GFP.
source: SUMOylation is restored to wild-type levels in UBQ:PPa5-GFP and slightly enhanced in UBQ:AVP1 plants indicating that low PPi levels are critical for efficient SUMOylation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SUMOylation is slightly enhanced in UBQ:AVP1 plants.
source: SUMOylation is restored to wild-type levels in UBQ:PPa5-GFP and slightly enhanced in UBQ:AVP1 plants indicating that low PPi levels are critical for efficient SUMOylation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Low PPi levels are critical for efficient SUMOylation.
source: SUMOylation is restored to wild-type levels in UBQ:PPa5-GFP and slightly enhanced in UBQ:AVP1 plants indicating that low PPi levels are critical for efficient SUMOylation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is inferred from the restoration of SUMOylation by PPa5-GFP and enhancement by AVP1.

claim: Rapid and reversible accumulation of SUMO conjugates occurs during heat stress.
source: Rapid and reversible accumulation of SUMO conjugates does not only occur during cold stress but also during heat stress (Miller et al., 2010; Rytz et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2010 and Rytz et al., 2018.

claim: Survival rate of fugu5 seedlings was strongly reduced by exposure to 40°C for 30 min.
source: Indeed, survival rate of fugu5 seedlings was strongly reduced by exposure to 40°C for 30 min but restored in the UBQ:PPa5-GFP complementation line.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Heat stress survival was restored in the UBQ:PPa5-GFP complementation line.
source: Indeed, survival rate of fugu5 seedlings was strongly reduced by exposure to 40°C for 30 min but restored in the UBQ:PPa5-GFP complementation line.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The survival rate of the UBQ:AVP1 overexpression line was increased compared to the wt after heat stress.
source: Of note, the survival rate of the UBQ:AVP1 overexpression line was increased compared to the wt (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Exposure to 40°C for 30 min led to accumulation of SUMO conjugates in the wt.
source: Exposure to 40°C for 30 min led to accumulation of SUMO conjugates in the wt, whereas the response was strongly reduced in fugu5-1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The heat-induced accumulation of SUMO conjugates was strongly reduced in fugu5-1.
source: Exposure to 40°C for 30 min led to accumulation of SUMO conjugates in the wt, whereas the response was strongly reduced in fugu5-1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A reduction of SUMO levels after heat stress was observed for fugu5-3.
source: Consistently, a reduction of SUMO levels after heat stress was also observed for fugu5-3 but was restored to wt levels in UBQ:PPa5-GFP and UBQ:AVP1 plants (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SUMO levels after heat stress were restored to wt levels in UBQ:PPa5-GFP plants.
source: Consistently, a reduction of SUMO levels after heat stress was also observed for fugu5-3 but was restored to wt levels in UBQ:PPa5-GFP and UBQ:AVP1 plants (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SUMO levels after heat stress were restored to wt levels in UBQ:AVP1 plants.
source: Consistently, a reduction of SUMO levels after heat stress was also observed for fugu5-3 but was restored to wt levels in UBQ:PPa5-GFP and UBQ:AVP1 plants (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SUMO plays an important role in stress responses across all eukaryotes.
source: SUMO plays an important role in stress responses across all eukaryotes (Enserink, 2015; Hannich et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Enserink, 2015 and Hannich et al., 2005.

claim: Switching the carbon source from galactose to glucose led to a depletion of IPP1 in the conditional yeast strain.
source: We employed a strain in which the sole and essential sPPase IPP1 is expressed under the control of the GAL1 promoter (Serrano-Bueno et al., 2013) so that switching the carbon source from galactose to glucose led to a depletion of IPP1 (Figure 5A) after 6 hr that was almost complete after 15 hr (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and citation to Serrano-Bueno et al., 2013.

claim: IPP1 depletion was almost complete after 15 hr in the conditional yeast strain.
source: We employed a strain in which the sole and essential sPPase IPP1 is expressed under the control of the GAL1 promoter (Serrano-Bueno et al., 2013) so that switching the carbon source from galactose to glucose led to a depletion of IPP1 (Figure 5A) after 6 hr that was almost complete after 15 hr (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Heat stress (40°C, 1 hr) increased SUMOylation by a factor of two in wt yeast.
source: When wt yeast was subjected to heat stress (40°C, 1 hr), SUMOylation increased by a factor of two (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Heat-induced SUMOylation was strongly diminished by depletion of IPP1 in yeast.
source: Heat-induced SUMOylation was strongly diminished by depletion of IPP1, (Figure 5C) indicating that inhibition of SUMOylation by PPi is not limited to plants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Inhibition of SUMOylation by PPi is not limited to plants.
source: Heat-induced SUMOylation was strongly diminished by depletion of IPP1, (Figure 5C) indicating that inhibition of SUMOylation by PPi is not limited to plants.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of reduced SUMOylation in yeast upon IPP1 depletion.

claim: Conjugation of SUMO to target proteins is initiated by E1 enzymes through adenylation, a reaction that releases PPi.
source: Conjugation of SUMO to target proteins is initiated by E1 enzymes through adenylation, a reaction that releases PPi and could thus be inhibited by increased cytosolic PPi levels (Haas et al., 1982; Lois and Lima, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Haas et al., 1982 and Lois and Lima, 2005.

claim: E1 enzyme adenylation could be inhibited by increased cytosolic PPi levels.
source: Conjugation of SUMO to target proteins is initiated by E1 enzymes through adenylation, a reaction that releases PPi and could thus be inhibited by increased cytosolic PPi levels (Haas et al., 1982; Lois and Lima, 2005).
evidence: This is speculated based on the reversibility of the adenylation reaction and supported by citations.

claim: Addition of micromolar concentrations of PPi caused a strong inhibition of CFP-RanGAPtail SUMOylation by the human E1 and E2.
source: Addition of micromolar concentrations of PPi caused a strong inhibition of CFP-RanGAPtail SUMOylation by the human E1 (Uba2/Aos1) and E2 (Ubc9) which could be released by addition of a soluble pyrophosphatase (Figure 6B + 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B + 6C.

claim: Inhibition of CFP-RanGAPtail SUMOylation by PPi could be released by addition of a soluble pyrophosphatase.
source: Addition of micromolar concentrations of PPi caused a strong inhibition of CFP-RanGAPtail SUMOylation by the human E1 (Uba2/Aos1) and E2 (Ubc9) which could be released by addition of a soluble pyrophosphatase (Figure 6B + 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B + 6C.

claim: Inhibition of E1E2 activity by PPi follows a mixed mode.
source: To determine the mode of inhibition, we determined Vmax and Km in the absence as well as in the presence of PPi (Figure 6B) leading to the conclusion that inhibition of E1E2 activity by PPi follows a mixed mode (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, 6D, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Arabidopsis SUMO E1-activity is inhibited by 10 µM PPi.
source: In accordance with the results for the human enzyme, the Arabidopsis SUMO E1-activity is inhibited by 10 µM PPi (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The combined action of V-ATPase and V-PPase enables plants to maintain transport into the vacuole even under stressful conditions.
source: It has long been assumed that the combined action of V-ATPase and V-PPase enables plants to maintain transport into the vacuole even under stressful conditions (Maeshima, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maeshima, 2000.

claim: Lack of the V-PPase limits cold acclimation severely.
source: We show here that lack of the V-PPase indeed limits cold acclimation severely.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1).

claim: Complementation by overexpression of the soluble pyrophosphatase PPa5 shows that the cold acclimation phenotype is not caused by a reduced proton-gradient.
source: However complementation by overexpression of the soluble pyrophosphatase PPa5 shows clearly that this phenotype is not caused by a reduced proton-gradient limiting cold-induced accumulation of solutes in the vacuole (Figure 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of cold acclimation by PPa5 expression and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Accumulation of PPi has been shown to be causative for the developmental phenotype of fugu5 seedlings.
source: Accumulation of PPi has been shown to be causative for the developmental phenotype of fugu5 seedlings (Ferjani et al., 2018; Ferjani et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ferjani et al., 2018 and Ferjani et al., 2011.

claim: Accumulation of PPi is causative for the freezing tolerance and heat stress phenotypes of fugu5.
source: and our results show that this also applies to the freezing tolerance and heat stress phenotypes caused by the lack of AVP1 that we report here for the first time.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 1 and 4).

claim: Overexpression of AVP1 results in increased stress tolerance and yield in multiple crop plants.
source: Although overexpression of AVP1 has been shown to result in increased stress tolerance and yield in multiple crop plants, reduced stress tolerance of fugu5 mutants has so far not been reported.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Reduced stress tolerance of fugu5 mutants has not been reported prior to this study.
source: Although overexpression of AVP1 has been shown to result in increased stress tolerance and yield in multiple crop plants, reduced stress tolerance of fugu5 mutants has so far not been reported.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings in this manuscript.

claim: The seedling phenotype of fugu5 seedlings could be rescued by supply of exogenous sucrose.
source: The fact that the seedling phenotype observable during the heterotrophic phase of fugu5 seedlings could be rescued by supply of exogenous sucrose pointed to an inhibition of gluconeogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The Glc1P/UDP-Glc reaction is reversible.
source: The Glc1P/UDP-Glc reaction is reversible and it has been shown that UGP-Glc pyrophosphorylase is a major target of PPi-inhibition during seedling establishment (Ferjani et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ferjani et al., 2018.

claim: UGP-Glc pyrophosphorylase is a major target of PPi-inhibition during seedling establishment.
source: The Glc1P/UDP-Glc reaction is reversible and it has been shown that UGP-Glc pyrophosphorylase is a major target of PPi-inhibition during seedling establishment (Ferjani et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ferjani et al., 2018.

claim: The early transcriptional response to cold is dampened in the fugu5 mutant.
source: the fact that the early transcriptional response to cold is dampened in the fugu5 mutant is not easily explained solely by a shift in sugar metabolism (Gutiérrez-Luna et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 and citation to Gutiérrez-Luna et al., 2018.

claim: PPi is released by E1 enzymes that initiate the attachment of ubiquitin or ubiquitin-like proteins (UBLs) including SUMO.
source: PPi is not only released by many anabolic reactions but also by E1 enzymes that initiate the attachment of ubiquitin or ubiquitin-like proteins (UBLs) including SUMO.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E1 enzyme mechanism.

claim: Activation of UBLs requires ATP and occurs via carboxy-terminal adenylation and thiol transfer leading to the release of AMP and PPi.
source: Activation of UBLs requires ATP and occurs via carboxy-terminal adenylation and thiol transfer leading to the release of AMP and PPi and would thus be prone to inhibition by PPi accumulation (Desterro et al., 1999; Schulman and Harper, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Desterro et al., 1999 and Schulman and Harper, 2009.

claim: UBL activation would be prone to inhibition by PPi accumulation.
source: Activation of UBLs requires ATP and occurs via carboxy-terminal adenylation and thiol transfer leading to the release of AMP and PPi and would thus be prone to inhibition by PPi accumulation (Desterro et al., 1999; Schulman and Harper, 2009).
evidence: This is speculated based on the reversibility of the adenylation reaction.

claim: ICE1 is subject to ubiquitination-mediated proteolysis under ambient temperature.
source: The MYC-like bHLH transcriptional activator ICE1 is subject to ubiquitination-mediated proteolysis under ambient temperature that is counteracted by SUMOylation during the cold response (Miura and Hasegawa, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miura and Hasegawa, 2008.

claim: Ubiquitination-mediated proteolysis of ICE1 is counteracted by SUMOylation during the cold response.
source: The MYC-like bHLH transcriptional activator ICE1 is subject to ubiquitination-mediated proteolysis under ambient temperature that is counteracted by SUMOylation during the cold response (Miura and Hasegawa, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miura and Hasegawa, 2008.

claim: The compromised cold acclimation of fugu5 is likely caused by the failure to stabilize ICE1.
source: We have shown here that the compromised cold acclimation of fugu5 is likely caused by the failure to stabilize ICE1 and that the overall levels of SUMO-conjugates that rapidly increase upon cold exposure in the wild-type fail to increase in fugu5 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The overall levels of SUMO-conjugates that rapidly increase upon cold exposure in the wild-type fail to increase in fugu5.
source: We have shown here that the compromised cold acclimation of fugu5 is likely caused by the failure to stabilize ICE1 and that the overall levels of SUMO-conjugates that rapidly increase upon cold exposure in the wild-type fail to increase in fugu5 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The rapid and reversible accumulation of SUMO conjugates is one of the fastest molecular responses observed during heat stress.
source: The rapid and reversible accumulation of SUMO conjugates is one of the fastest molecular responses observed during heat stress (Kurepa et al., 2003; Rytz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kurepa et al., 2003 and Rytz et al., 2018.

claim: The heat stress response of SUMO accumulation is dampened in both plants and yeast when PPi accumulates.
source: The fact that this response is dampened in both plants and yeast when PPi accumulates (Figures 4 and 5) argues strongly against a secondary metabolic effect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The dampened heat stress response in plants and yeast argues strongly against a secondary metabolic effect.
source: The fact that this response is dampened in both plants and yeast when PPi accumulates (Figures 4 and 5) argues strongly against a secondary metabolic effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of the effect across different organisms.

claim: The SUMOylation of RanGAP catalysed by human E1 and E2 enzymes was inhibited by micromolar concentrations of PPi following a mixed mode of inhibition.
source: Evidence for a direct inhibitory effect of PPi on SUMOylation was obtained in an in vitro FRET-based assay that allowed us to determine that the SUMOylation of RanGAP catalysed by human E1 and E2 enzymes was inhibited by micromolar concentrations of PPi following a mixed mode of inhibition (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The reaction catalysed by the heterodimeric E1 activating enzyme releases PPi.
source: Although we cannot exclude that PPi could inhibit the action of the E2 enzyme, the reaction catalysed by the heterodimeric E1 activating enzyme releases PPi and is thus most likely inhibited when PPi accumulates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E1 enzyme mechanism.

claim: The E1 activating enzyme is most likely inhibited when PPi accumulates.
source: Although we cannot exclude that PPi could inhibit the action of the E2 enzyme, the reaction catalysed by the heterodimeric E1 activating enzyme releases PPi and is thus most likely inhibited when PPi accumulates.
evidence: This is inferred from the reversibility of the E1 adenylation reaction.

claim: E1 subunit SAE2 ~SUMO thioester formation is inhibited in the presence of micromolar PPi.
source: Indeed, we could show that E1 subunit SAE2 ~SUMO thioester formation is inhibited in the presence of micromolar PPi, raising the question how exactly PPi inhibits E1-activity (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: For adenylation of the SUMO C-terminus to occur, the E1 enzyme adopts an open conformation that allows binding of ATP.
source: For adenylation of the SUMO C-terminus to occur, the E1 enzyme adopts an open conformation that allows binding of ATP.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E1 enzyme mechanism.

claim: In the open conformation, the catalytic cysteine of E1 is too far away and unavailable to become linked to SUMO.
source: In this conformation, the catalytic cysteine of E1 is too far away and unavailable to become linked to SUMO.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E1 enzyme mechanism.

claim: Thioester bond formation between E1 and SUMO requires structural remodelling to a closed conformation.
source: Thioester bond formation between E1 and SUMO requires structural remodelling to a closed conformation in which the catalytic cysteine moves adjacent to the C terminus of SUMO ~AMP, via unfolding of structures associated with ATP binding and SUMO adenylation (Lois and Lima, 2005; Olsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lois and Lima, 2005 and Olsen et al., 2010.

claim: Active site remodelling pushes the E1 reaction forward by promoting the release of pyrophosphate to prevent the reverse reaction.
source: It has been suggested that active site remodelling pushes the E1 reaction forward by promoting the release of pyrophosphate to prevent the reverse reaction, the attack of the adenylate by pyrophosphate leading to the reformation of ATP.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E1 enzyme mechanism.

claim: The adenylation step is rate limiting for E1 enzymes.
source: Not only is the adenylation step rate limiting, once the thioester bond is formed and AMP is released, E1 switches back to the open conformation and a second adenylation reaction occurs, resulting in the formation of a ternary complex, with an E1 molecule binding to one SUMO molecule at the adenylation active site and to a second via a thioester bond through the catalytic cysteine (Olsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Olsen et al., 2010.

claim: Once the thioester bond is formed and AMP is released, E1 switches back to the open conformation and a second adenylation reaction occurs.
source: Not only is the adenylation step rate limiting, once the thioester bond is formed and AMP is released, E1 switches back to the open conformation and a second adenylation reaction occurs, resulting in the formation of a ternary complex, with an E1 molecule binding to one SUMO molecule at the adenylation active site and to a second via a thioester bond through the catalytic cysteine (Olsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Olsen et al., 2010.

claim: E1 enzymes are potential targets for therapeutic intervention in cancer and other diseases.
source: As E1 enzymes are potential targets for therapeutic intervention in cancer and other diseases understanding their enzymatic activity as well as inhibitory mechanisms at the atomic level may provide leads for the development of novel drugs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the therapeutic potential of E1 enzyme inhibitors.

claim: A novel allosteric inhibitor that targets a cryptic pocket distinct from the active site and locks the enzyme in a previously unobserved inactive conformation has been identified for E1 enzymes.
source: A novel allosteric inhibitor that targets a cryptic pocket distinct from the active site and locks the enzyme in a previously unobserved inactive conformation has recently been identified (Lv et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lv et al., 2018.

claim: E1 activity is classically measured as ATP:PPi exchange.
source: Although the exact mechanism remains to be determined, the fact that E1 activity is classically measured as ATP:PPi (Haas et al., 1982; Haas and Rose, 1982) exchange clearly reflects that inhibition of E1 enzymes by PPi is not novel per se.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Haas et al., 1982 and Haas and Rose, 1982.

claim: Inhibition of E1 enzymes by PPi is not novel per se.
source: Although the exact mechanism remains to be determined, the fact that E1 activity is classically measured as ATP:PPi (Haas et al., 1982; Haas and Rose, 1982) exchange clearly reflects that inhibition of E1 enzymes by PPi is not novel per se.
evidence: This is inferred from the use of ATP:PPi exchange assays to measure E1 activity.

claim: The relevance of inhibition by PPi in vivo has not been addressed prior to this study.
source: Although cytosolic PPi concentrations reported in the literature, in particular for plants, strongly suggest that relevant concentrations occur not only in mutant backgrounds or under stress conditions the relevance of inhibition by PPi in vivo has so far not been addressed.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings in this manuscript.

claim: Cytosolic PPi concentrations of 0.2–0.3 mM as reported for spinach leaves would not be compatible with E1 activity.
source: Cytosolic PPi concentrations of 0.2–0.3 mM as reported for spinach leaves (Weiner et al., 1987) would clearly not be compatible with E1 activity suggesting that PPi levels are maintained at substantially lower levels at least in the immediate environment of E1 enzymes.
evidence: This is inferred from the inhibitory effect of PPi on E1 activity and supported by citation to Weiner et al., 1987.

claim: PPi levels are maintained at substantially lower levels at least in the immediate environment of E1 enzymes.
source: Cytosolic PPi concentrations of 0.2–0.3 mM as reported for spinach leaves (Weiner et al., 1987) would clearly not be compatible with E1 activity suggesting that PPi levels are maintained at substantially lower levels at least in the immediate environment of E1 enzymes.
evidence: This is inferred from the incompatibility of high PPi concentrations with E1 activity.

claim: Many nuclear proteins are modified by SUMOylation.
source: Many nuclear proteins are modified by SUMOylation (Rytz et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rytz et al., 2018.

claim: The SUMO conjugation complex self-assembles into nuclear bodies.
source: and the SUMO conjugation complex self-assembles into nuclear bodies (Mazur et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mazur et al., 2019.

claim: DNA and RNA synthesis occurs against high concentrations of PPi.
source: the fact that DNA and RNA synthesis occurs against such high concentrations of PPi argues not only that soluble pyrophosphatases play an important role in the nucleus but could also suggest that nuclear PPase activity is higher than in the cytosol.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for PPi removal during nucleic acid synthesis.

claim: Soluble pyrophosphatases play an important role in the nucleus.
source: the fact that DNA and RNA synthesis occurs against such high concentrations of PPi argues not only that soluble pyrophosphatases play an important role in the nucleus but could also suggest that nuclear PPase activity is higher than in the cytosol.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for PPi removal during nucleic acid synthesis.

claim: Nuclear PPase activity might be higher than in the cytosol.
source: the fact that DNA and RNA synthesis occurs against such high concentrations of PPi argues not only that soluble pyrophosphatases play an important role in the nucleus but could also suggest that nuclear PPase activity is higher than in the cytosol.
evidence: This is speculated based on the requirement for PPi removal during nucleic acid synthesis.

claim: A quadruple knockout mutant lacking four of five PPa-isoforms showed no obvious growth phenotype.
source: However, the fact that a quadruple knockout mutant lacking four of five PPa-isoforms showed no obvious growth phenotype whereas the combined loss of the H+-PPase AVP1 and a single PPa-isoform causes severe dwarfism due to high PPi concentrations (Segami et al., 2018) shows clearly that cytosolic and nuclear pools of PPi are controlled by the combined action of s PPase and H+-PPase.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Segami et al., 2018.

claim: The combined loss of the H+-PPase AVP1 and a single PPa-isoform causes severe dwarfism due to high PPi concentrations.
source: However, the fact that a quadruple knockout mutant lacking four of five PPa-isoforms showed no obvious growth phenotype whereas the combined loss of the H+-PPase AVP1 and a single PPa-isoform causes severe dwarfism due to high PPi concentrations (Segami et al., 2018) shows clearly that cytosolic and nuclear pools of PPi are controlled by the combined action of s PPase and H+-PPase.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Segami et al., 2018.

claim: Cytosolic and nuclear pools of PPi are controlled by the combined action of sPPase and H+-PPase.
source: However, the fact that a quadruple knockout mutant lacking four of five PPa-isoforms showed no obvious growth phenotype whereas the combined loss of the H+-PPase AVP1 and a single PPa-isoform causes severe dwarfism due to high PPi concentrations (Segami et al., 2018) shows clearly that cytosolic and nuclear pools of PPi are controlled by the combined action of s PPase and H+-PPase.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic data and supported by citation to Segami et al., 2018.

claim: Converting the substantial energy present in PPi into a proton-gradient seems preferable to releasing it as heat for plants.
source: At least for plants, converting the substantial energy present in PPi into a proton-gradient seems preferable to releasing it as heat and the soluble PPases might thus only function as emergency valves.
evidence: This is speculated based on the presence of H+-PPases in plants.

claim: The soluble PPases might only function as emergency valves.
source: At least for plants, converting the substantial energy present in PPi into a proton-gradient seems preferable to releasing it as heat and the soluble PPases might thus only function as emergency valves.
evidence: This is speculated based on the presence of H+-PPases in plants.

claim: Four PPa-isoforms are transcriptionally up-regulated during the first six hours of the cold acclimation response.
source: The fact that four PPa-isoforms are transcriptionally up-regulated during the first six hours of the cold acclimation response (Figure 2) indicates that control of PPi levels is an integral part of the cold stress response
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Control of PPi levels is an integral part of the cold stress response.
source: The fact that four PPa-isoforms are transcriptionally up-regulated during the first six hours of the cold acclimation response (Figure 2) indicates that control of PPi levels is an integral part of the cold stress response
evidence: This is inferred from the upregulation of PPa-isoforms during cold stress.

claim: Constitutive overexpression of AVP1 causes increased growth of diverse crop plants under various abiotic stress conditions.
source: Constitutive overexpression of AVP1 has been shown to cause increased growth of diverse crop plants under various abiotic stress conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Greater vacuolar ion sequestration has been proposed to explain aspects of the phenotypes observed in plants lacking or over-expressing AVP1.
source: Greater vacuolar ion sequestration, increased auxin transport, enhanced heterotrophic growth, and increased source to sink transport of sucrose have all been proposed to explain individual aspects of the phenotypes observed in plants lacking or over-expressing AVP1 (Park et al., 2005; Pasapula et al., 2011; Schilling et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Park et al., 2005, Pasapula et al., 2011, Schilling et al., 2017, and Yang et al., 2014.

claim: Modulation of SUMOylation by cellular pyrophosphate levels is proposed as a unifying hypothesis that might explain both the stress-related and developmental aspects of the multifaceted AVP1 loss- and gain-of function phenotypes.
source: Here, we propose modulation of SUMOylation by cellular pyrophosphate levels as a unifying hypothesis that might explain both, the stress-related as well as the developmental aspects of the multifaceted AVP1 loss- and gain-of function phenotypes.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings.

claim: A combination of tissue-specific and inducible expression of PPi-hydrolysing enzymes might be an efficient way of generating stress-tolerant crops.
source: Although our hypothesis needs further experimental validation in particular regarding the developmental phenotypes, it seems obvious that a combination of tissue-specific and inducible expression of PPi-hydrolysing enzymes might turn out to be an efficient way of generating stress-tolerant crops for the future.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings of the study.
